overview.intro: With the end of the cold war one power stood without a peer, and the resulting order tested how a single dominant state behaves and how others respond. This unit examines the meaning and features of a unipolar world and the unilateralism it permitted, the case studies of Iraq and Afghanistan through which American power was exercised, and India’s changing relationship with the United States in defence and trade after 1991.

facts.label: Unipolarity
facts.value: A distribution of power in which one state faces no peer competitor and can act without balancing by an opposite coalition.

facts.label: Iraq
facts.value: 1991 Gulf War after the invasion of Kuwait; 2003 invasion and occupation; sanctions in the interval.

facts.label: Afghanistan
facts.value: 2001 intervention after the September attacks, followed by a long counter-insurgency and withdrawal in 2021.

facts.label: India–USA
facts.value: From non-alignment and sanctions to the 2005 nuclear agreement, defence agreements and a large trade relationship.

learningOutcomes: Define a unipolar world and explain its features.
Explain unilateralism and its consequences for the international order.
Use Iraq and Afghanistan as case studies of unipolar power.
Trace the development of India’s defence and trade relations with the USA after 1991.

learn.title: Meaning and features of a unipolar world

blocks.text: Polarity describes how power is distributed among the leading states. Unipolarity describes a system in which one state is so far ahead in military, economic and institutional capacity that no coalition of the others can balance it without joining it. The unipolar moment after 1991 rested on specific advantages: a military without rival in power-projection, the dollar as the reserve currency, leadership of the principal international institutions, technological dominance in the emerging digital economy, and alliances that gave the dominant power bases across every region.

The features of such a system follow from that position. The dominant state can act unilaterally with far less cost than in a balance-of-power system, since no counter-coalition forms quickly enough to raise the price of action. Alliances become easier to assemble but harder to refuse, because the lesser partner has no alternative patron. The dominant state also carries disproportionate burdens — the maintenance of sea lanes, financial stability, crisis intervention — which is the paradox of primacy: it is powerful enough to act alone and expected to act on everyone’s behalf. Critics add that unipolarity tempts overreach, since a power that faces no immediate constraint tends to confuse what is possible with what is wise.

blocks.text: Unilateralism is the conduct of foreign policy by a state acting on its own judgment without alliance consultation or institutional authorisation. In a unipolar order it becomes attractive because consultation is optional: the dominant state can set the timetable, define the threat and act before agreement catches up. Its instruments include military action without Security Council authorisation, sanctions applied independently, withdrawal from treaties and agreements, and the use of economic leverage to compel changes in other states’ policies.

The consequences are double-edged. Unilateral action can be decisive where institutions are slow, as in the rapid response to the invasion of Kuwait in 1991, and it can supply public goods that no coalition would fund. But it also corrodes the legitimacy on which long-term leadership rests: action without authorisation invites the charge that the rules bind others and not the power that wrote them, and unilateral measures that fail — the occupation of Iraq being the clearest example — impose costs on allies as well as on the acting state. The institutional reply is that authorisation through the United Nations and consultation within alliances convert power into legitimate authority, and that a unipolar moment lasts only while others accept the burdens and the leadership; the gradual emergence of a more contested order through the 2000s suggests the point at which the costs began to exceed the benefits.

items: Unilateralism thrives when no counter-coalition can form quickly.
It can act faster than institutions, which is its genuine advantage.
It corrodes legitimacy when the rules appear to bind only other states.
Failure costs allies as well as the acting power, which erodes alliances.
Legitimacy, not capacity, determines how long primacy lasts.

blocks.text: Iraq supplies two episodes. In August 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait, and a coalition authorised by the United Nations Security Council expelled it by March 1991 in a war that demonstrated American capacity to assemble and lead an international coalition; sanctions then remained in place through the 1990s over disputes about weapons inspection. The second episode, the invasion of 2003, was conducted without Security Council authorisation after the failure to secure a second resolution, on the stated grounds of weapons of mass destruction that were not found and of a connection to terrorism that was not established. Occupation brought insurgency, sectarian conflict and state collapse, and the intervention divided European allies, weakened the case for multilateral authorisation and accelerated the retreat from unilateralism.

Afghanistan began differently: the intervention of October 2001 followed the September attacks and enjoyed broad international support and a Security Council basis, since the right of self-defence was invoked with unusual unanimity. The mission then expanded from counter-terrorism into state-building and counter-insurgency, which required a long presence, competing insurgent sanctuaries and fragile institutions, and after two decades the United States withdrew in 2011 in a departure that ended the campaign without the political settlement it had sought. Read together, the two cases show a pattern rather than an accident: initial capacity to act rapidly, followed by the difficulty of converting military success into political order, followed by declining domestic and allied support for open-ended commitments.

learn.title: India’s defence and trade relations with the USA after 1991

blocks.text: India’s relationship with the United States moved through three phases after 1991. The first was the residue of non-alignment: the end of the cold war removed India’s value as a counterweight, defence procurement continued by inheritance from Russia, and the nuclear tests of 1998 brought sanctions that froze the relationship at its lowest point. The second was recovery from the late 1990s, driven by India’s economic liberalisation, the strategic interest in a democratic partner in Asia, and shared concern about terrorism and proliferation, which turned confrontation into dialogue within a few years.

The third phase has been consolidation. The civil nuclear agreement of 2005 resolved the principal dispute by recognising India’s civilian programme while connecting it to the international regime, and it was followed by defence agreements covering logistics, intelligence and joint production, by regular naval and army exercises, and by technology arrangements that treat India as a partner rather than a suspect. Trade and investment have expanded on the back of the technology and services sectors, though the relationship still carries friction over agricultural access, tariffs and India’s energy purchases elsewhere. The structural continuity beneath the phases is that both countries are large democracies in an region where power is concentrating, which gives the partnership a logic that survives changes of government in either capital.

blocks.caption: Three phases of India–USA relations after 1991
rows: Cold war usefulness gone; sanctions after the 1998 tests
Dialogue restored; strategic and economic interests converge
Civil nuclear agreement, defence logistics, exercises, technology partnership

items: Defence ties shifted from confrontation and suspicion to interoperability and joint exercise.
The 2005 civil nuclear agreement was the turning point that removed the principal dispute.
Trade is concentrated in technology, services, energy and manufactured goods.
Friction continues over market access, tariffs and each side’s relations with third countries.
The partnership’s logic rests on democracy, balance in Asia and economic complementarity.

questions.prompt: A unipolar world is one in which:
options: One state has no peer competitor
questions.answer: One state has no peer competitor
questions.explanation: Polarity describes the distribution of power, and unipolarity describes a single dominant state without a counterweight.

questions.prompt: The 2003 invasion of Iraq was distinctive because it:
options: Was conducted without a second Security Council resolution
Was led by the United Nations
questions.answer: Was conducted without a second Security Council resolution
questions.explanation: The coalition acted without a second resolution after the failure to secure one, which divided allies and damaged the case for multilateral authorisation.

questions.prompt: India’s relations with the USA in the decade after 1991 were constrained chiefly by:
options: Non-alignment’s legacy and the 1998 nuclear sanctions
questions.answer: Non-alignment’s legacy and the 1998 nuclear sanctions
questions.explanation: The end of the cold war removed India’s counterweight value and the 1998 tests froze the relationship before the recovery of the late 1990s.

questions.prompt: The main lesson drawn from both Iraq and Afghanistan is that:
options: Rapid military success does not by itself produce political order
questions.answer: Rapid military success does not by itself produce political order
questions.explanation: Both episodes show initial military success followed by insurgency, state-building difficulty and declining support for open-ended commitments.

questions.prompt: Conducting foreign policy without consulting allies or seeking institutional authorisation is called __________ .
questions.explanation: It becomes attractive in a unipolar order because no counter-coalition forms quickly to raise the cost of action.

questions.prompt: The rapid response to the invasion of Kuwait in 1991 was a coalition authorised by the United Nations Security __________ .
questions.explanation: The 1991 operation is the standard example of multilateral authorisation working within a unipolar distribution of power.

questions.prompt: State four features of a unipolar world.
questions.answer: Four features are: no peer competitor, so action proceeds without a balancing coalition to raise its cost; institutional leadership, which lets the dominant state shape the rules of the system; alliance dependence, since lesser partners have no alternative patron and find refusal difficult; and the burden of primacy, whereby the dominant state is expected to maintain sea lanes, financial stability and crisis response. The temptation to overreach because constraints are weak is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each feature must be paired with the consequence it produces.

questions.prompt: Compare India’s defence and trade relations with the USA before and after the turn of the century.
questions.answer: Before the turn of the century the relationship was constrained. Non-alignment had made India useful as a counterweight during the cold war but dispensable afterwards, defence procurement continued by inheritance from Russia, economic liberalisation had barely begun, and the nuclear tests of 1998 brought sanctions that froze the relationship at its lowest point. After the turn of the century the relationship recovered and then deepened: strategic dialogue resumed from the late 1990s, the civilian nuclear agreement of 2005 resolved the principal dispute, defence cooperation moved from confrontation to interoperability and joint exercise, technology agreements followed, and trade and investment expanded substantially with the technology and services sectors at the centre. The change rested on three continuities of interest — a democratic partner in Asia, shared concern over terrorism and proliferation, and the economic complementarity of the two economies — so the difference was not of values, which had long been compatible, but of strategic alignment and economic integration.
questions.explanation: Two phases must be contrasted on defence and trade together, with dates and a reason for the change.

questions.prompt: Examine unilateralism as a feature of a unipolar world, with reference to Iraq and Afghanistan.
questions.answer: Unilateralism is the conduct of policy without alliance consultation or institutional authorisation, and in a unipolar order it becomes the default because no counter-coalition can form quickly enough to raise the price of acting. Its advantages are real: in 1991 the coalition assembled against the invasion of Kuwait moved rapidly, restored a member state and did so under Security Council authorisation, which shows that dominant power can be used to make collective decisions work rather than to bypass them. The pattern diverges in 2003, where the invasion of Iraq proceeded without a second resolution after the effort to secure one failed, on grounds of weapons of mass destruction that were not found and a terrorist connection that was not established. The costs were political rather than military: allies who had been consulted were divided or bypassed, the occupation produced insurgency and sectarian collapse, and the legitimacy of the whole framework of collective security was weakened because the rules appeared to bind everyone except the power that had helped write them. Afghanistan began with an unusual degree of authorisation, the right of self-defence invoked after the September attacks with Security Council acquiescence, but the mission expanded from counter-terrorism into state-building and counter-insurgency, and after two decades the withdrawal of 2021 ended it without the political settlement sought. Read together the cases establish three propositions: unilateral action is fastest at the start, legitimacy is what determines whether others carry the cost, and military success does not convert into political order without institutions that only the aftermath provides. The assessment must therefore distinguish the instrument from its authorisation — force was decisive in Kuwait and inconclusive in Iraq — and judge unilateralism by whether it strengthens or erodes the coalition that gives primacy its durability.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both case studies with dates and authorisation status, the advantage of unilateralism stated, and a judgement linking legitimacy to the duration of unipolarity.

questions.prompt: Is a unipolar moment self-limiting? Discuss with reference to the behaviour of the dominant state and the responses of other powers.
questions.answer: The case that it is self-limiting rests on a mechanism rather than a forecast. Primacy is expensive: the dominant state must maintain sea lanes, underwrite financial stability, lead interventions and sustain alliances, and the burdens accumulate while the benefits accrue disproportionately to allies who can under-spend on defence — the classic free-rider problem, and the reason complaints about burden-sharing appear in every administration. Second, unilateral conduct corrodes the legitimacy that makes leadership cheap: each bypass of an alliance or institution teaches partners to hedge, to build alternative arrangements and to resist the next request, so the coalition that multiplies the power of the dominant state gradually thins. Third, absence of a peer competitor removes the discipline that keeps strategy proportionate: without an immediate cost for miscalculation, interventions are undertaken on marginal interests and open-ended commitments accumulate, as Iraq and Afghanistan demonstrate. The responses of other powers reinforce the mechanism: hedging by allies, the creation of alternative institutions and financial arrangements by rising states, and coalition-building by those who prefer a more contested order all reduce the margin of freedom the dominant state began with. The case against runs on capacity rather than behaviour. A gap of the scale that existed after 1991 — in military reach, reserve currency, technology and institutional leadership — does not close quickly, and no balancing coalition has yet formed that could match the dominant state in more than one region; recent efforts at multipolar coordination have been shallow where interests diverge, which suggests that the balance of power tends to reassert itself more slowly than its critics expect. The most defensible conclusion is that unipolarity is self-limiting in legitimacy and burden long before it is self-limiting in capacity: the dominant state can remain the strongest power for decades while ceasing to be able to set the terms of events, which is precisely the condition that began to appear after the interventions of the 2000s. The answer should therefore distinguish the distribution of material power from the durability of leadership built on it, and use both to reach a reasoned judgement.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the mechanism of self-limitation specified in burden, legitimacy and overreach, the counter-case on capacity, and a judgement that separates material primacy from the ability to lead.
